newsitem.title: USA: U.S. House Democrat, Wirth debate climate change.
newsitem.headline: U.S. House Democrat, Wirth debate climate change.

text.p: The Clinton administration has locked itself into a negotiating stance in world climate change talks without understanding global warming or knowing how measures it is advocating will affect the economy, the top House Commerce Committee Democrat said Wednesday.

"How do we conduct an intelligent negotiation without understanding the facts in full?" Representative John Dingell of Michigan said in a debate with the administration's leading official on the climate change talks, Under Secretary of State Tim Wirth.
Wirth, in the discussion held by a Washington think tank, said there is enough evidence that industrial pollution will change the climate to start taking steps to cut emissions.
He also said the administration will produce a long-promised analysis of the economic impact of reducing carbon emissions in March.

Dingell said the administration promised to provide that analysis before it made important decisions on international climate-change talks. But instead, he said, it has committed itself "to binding constraints" to reduce carbon emissions without imposing constraints on developing countries that are becoming major polluters and trade competitors.
"The analysis comes too late to properly inform the process, and likely will be used to justify what the administration has already decided to do," Dingell said.

Wirth said the economic analysis has been "extraordinarily difficult to do," and said the United States has not negotiated on numerical targets or timetables for cutting emissions before it has the analysis.

"We won't negotiate timetables and targets until we have the information fully in hand," Wirth said. He said the administration probably will not propose numerical targets and timetables until this summer.
The international talks are to culminate in December in Kyoto, Japan, where the United States and other countries hope to reach a binding agreement.
The administration proposed using a system of trading credits for reducing pollution to provide economic incentives for industrialised countries to meet specific emissions reductions targets.

Developing countries would not be bound by emissions reductions targets, but would be included in the process through "joint implementation" in which industrialised countries get credit for projects to curb developing countries' pollution.
"We fouled the nest. We have a responsibility for that," Wirth said of industrialised countries.
But Dingell said the administration's proposal sends a signal to developing countries to "hurry up, get your development going as fast as you can while you still can get away with it."
